Education only. Not for diagnosis, treatment or any clinical decision.

## In 60 seconds

Smartwatches and fitness trackers watch the pulse with light, and implanted monitors watch the
heart's electrical activity for years. Both run detectors around the clock, so even a small false
alarm rate per check adds up to many alerts. Wearables answer this by demanding several irregular
windows in a row before they notify [@lubitz2022]; clinics that follow implanted monitors answer it
with better detection algorithms and with people who review every alert [@neiman2024]. This module
derives three things an engineer needs here: how pulse timing differs from heartbeat timing, what
"k windows in a row" buys and costs, and how a triage filter trades review time against missed
events.

## From the field

- **Large wearable studies measured predictive value, not only accuracy.** In the Stanford-led
  Apple Heart Study, the watch's PPG sensor measured the pulse intermittently while the wearer was
  at rest. 2,161 of 419,297 participants (0.52%) received an irregular-pulse notification over a
  median of 117 days. Among those who returned an analyzable ECG patch, AF was present in
  34% [@perez2019].
- **The rule matters as much as the model.** The Fitbit Heart Study notified only after 11
  consecutive irregular 5-minute pulse windows. Of 225 participants with another such detection
  while wearing an ECG patch, 221 had AF at the same time: a positive predictive value of 98.2%
  [@lubitz2022].
- **Implanted monitors generate review work.** Historically about 75% of implantable loop recorder
  (ILR) alerts were false positives. In one surveillance program, two newer remotely
  reprogrammable ILR models with AI-based detection had 18.0% and 38.3% false-positive alerts
  [@neiman2024]. A systematic review found false alarms in 59.7% of remote transmissions, most often
  for AF, mainly triggered by premature beats [@covino2024].
- **Device electrograms can be classified too.** A Stanford team trained deep networks on
  intracardiac electrograms to tell AF from atrial tachycardia, which devices tend to lump together
  as high-rate events, and compared them with rate and regularity rules [@rodrigo2022]. A review
  covers AI across implanted devices: alert filtering, event prediction and programming
  [@antoun2025].
- **Agents are arriving.** An agent that called signal-processing tools estimated heart rate from
  PPG better than language models reading the numbers directly [@feli2025]. Another study used a
  language model to aggregate simulated pacemaker remote-monitoring data and estimate battery level
  [@iwai2025]. Module m44 covers how such agents are built and kept safe.

## Derivations

Symbols: $RR_i$ the $i$-th interval between R peaks (s), $\Delta_i$ the delay from R peak $i$ to
its pulse at the wrist (s), $\mathrm{IBI}_i$ the interval between pulses $i$ and $i+1$ (s), $q$ the
chance that a window in regular rhythm is judged irregular, $p$ the same chance in AF, $k$ the
number of irregular windows required in a row, $n$ windows per day, $L$ windows in an AF episode.

### Pulse timing is not heartbeat timing

**Photoplethysmography** (PPG) shines light into the skin and measures how much returns. The
pulsatile part of the signal follows the change in blood volume with each heartbeat, on top of a
slowly varying baseline [@allen2007]. Heart rate comes from the mean interval:

$$
\mathrm{HR} = \frac{60}{\overline{\mathrm{IBI}}} \quad \text{beats per minute}
$$ {#eq-m38-hr}

Each pulse reaches the wrist a delay $\Delta_i$ after its R peak, and that delay varies from beat to
beat. Subtracting successive pulse times gives an exact identity:

$$
\mathrm{IBI}_i = RR_i + \left(\Delta_{i+1} - \Delta_i\right)
$$ {#eq-m38-ibi}

If the delays are stationary, with variance $\sigma_\Delta^2$ and lag-one correlation $\rho$, and
independent of the RR intervals, then

$$
\operatorname{Var}(\mathrm{IBI}) = \operatorname{Var}(RR) + 2\sigma_\Delta^2\,(1 - \rho)
$$ {#eq-m38-ibi-var}

Pulse intervals are always at least as variable as heartbeat intervals. Delay jitter makes a regular
rhythm look a little irregular, and quick changes in delay ($\rho$ near 0) are worse than slow ones
($\rho$ near 1). Motion adds missed and extra pulses on top. A pulse-based irregularity detector
must allow for both.

**Key takeaways**

- PPG measures the pulse, not the heartbeat; its intervals add the change in pulse delay.
- Delay jitter inflates variability by $2\sigma_\Delta^2(1-\rho)$, so regular rhythm can look
  irregular.
- Thresholds tuned on ECG intervals do not transfer unchanged to PPG.

### Many windows a day: what "k in a row" buys

A wearable checks its data in windows, for example 5-minute windows, about 288 a day. Suppose each
window in regular rhythm is wrongly judged irregular with probability $q$, independently. If the
device notifies after $k$ irregular windows in a row, the expected number of false notifications in
$n$ windows (counting each run once) is

$$
\mathbb E[\text{runs}] = q^{k}\left[1 + (n - k)(1 - q)\right]
$$ {#eq-m38-runs}

A run of at least $k$ starts at the first window when the first $k$ windows are positive, and at a
later window when that window and the next $k-1$ are positive and the window before it is not.

The same rule can miss a short AF episode. If an episode spans $L$ windows, each flagged with
probability $p$, let $a_m$ be the probability of no run of $k$ in $m$ windows. Then $a_m = 1$ for
$m < k$, and

$$
a_m = \sum_{j=0}^{k-1} p^{j}(1 - p)\, a_{m-j-1}, \qquad P(\text{episode caught}) = 1 - a_L
$$ {#eq-m38-detect}

since a sequence with no run of $k$ must begin with $j < k$ flagged windows followed by an unflagged
one. Raising $k$ cuts false notifications geometrically, as $q^k$, but it also cuts the chance of
catching episodes shorter than a few times $k$ windows.

::: {.demo #m38-d1 badge="exact"}
```{=html}
<div id="m38-d1-root" class="demo-root" data-demo="m38-d1"></div>
<script type="module" src="../demos/m38-d1-consecutive-windows.js"></script>
```

**Assumptions**

- Model: @eq-m38-runs and @eq-m38-detect, exact when windows are judged independently with fixed $q$
  and $p$. Real windows are not independent: noise and motion come in bursts, and overlapping
  windows share data. Correlated false windows make false notifications more likely than
  @eq-m38-runs predicts (lab part E measures this on Holter data).
- All slider values are illustrative inputs. The 5-minute default window echoes the windows
  used in @lubitz2022; $q$, $p$ and the episode length are not taken from any study.
- What would change the result: windows that overlap, a rule that is not "k in a row" (for example
  "k of the last m"), or episodes that start and stop mid-window.
:::

**Key takeaways**

- Over a day of windows, small per-window false rates become daily alerts.
- "k in a row" divides false notifications by roughly $1/q$ per extra window required.
- It also misses short episodes; choose $k$ knowing which episodes matter.

### The review inbox

Every alert from an implanted monitor that reaches a clinic needs a person. With $N$ patients,
$\lambda$ alerts per patient per day, a fraction PPV of them true and $\tau$ minutes to review
each, the daily load is

$$
A = N\lambda, \qquad A_{\text{false}} = N\lambda\,(1 - \mathrm{PPV}), \qquad H = \frac{N\lambda\,\tau}{60}\ \text{hours}
$$ {#eq-m38-workload}

A triage filter, whether a better on-device algorithm or a model at the clinic, keeps a share
$\kappa$ of true alerts and removes a share $r$ of false ones. The alerts that remain have

$$
\mathrm{PPV}' = \frac{\kappa\,\mathrm{PPV}}{\kappa\,\mathrm{PPV} + (1 - r)(1 - \mathrm{PPV})}
$$ {#eq-m38-filter}

and $N\lambda\,\mathrm{PPV}(1-\kappa)$ true alerts a day are no longer seen by anyone. This is Bayes'
rule again ([m35](m35-machine-learning.qmd#eq-m35-ppv)), with the raw PPV in the role of prevalence,
$\kappa$ as sensitivity and $r$ as specificity.

::: {.demo #m38-d2 badge="exact"}
```{=html}
<div id="m38-d2-root" class="demo-root" data-demo="m38-d2"></div>
<script type="module" src="../demos/m38-d2-alert-inbox.js"></script>
```

**Assumptions**

- Model: @eq-m38-workload and @eq-m38-filter, exact for the stated rates. Alerts are treated as
  independent; review time per alert is constant.
- The default raw PPV of 25% corresponds to the historical figure of about 75% false-positive ILR
  alerts quoted by @neiman2024. Clinic size, alert rate, review minutes and the filter's $\kappa$ and
  $r$ are illustrative inputs.
- What would change the result: true alerts are not all equally important; a filter that hides a
  rare dangerous rhythm costs far more than one that hides a common benign one.
:::

**Key takeaways**

- Review time scales with alerts, not with patients who are ill.
- A filter's value is review time saved; its cost is true alerts no one sees.
- Report both $\kappa$ and $r$, and which kinds of true alerts are lost.

## Clinical correlate

::: {.callout-note title="Pending clinical review"}
This section describes published findings only. It is not guidance for patient care, and it has
not yet been reviewed by an EP physician.
:::

**False alerts from implanted loop recorders.** An implantable loop recorder (ILR) is a small
device placed under the skin that records the ECG for years and sends alerts when its detector
fires. A systematic review of 12 reports covering 3,305 patients followed by remote monitoring found
that false-positive alarms made up 59.7% of remote transmissions and affected about one patient in
five. False AF alarms were the most common type, mainly due to premature atrial and ventricular
beats [@covino2024].

A retrospective study of a national surveillance program looked at two remotely reprogrammable ILR
models with two-stage, AI-based detection [@neiman2024]. Every alert was reviewed by staff. False
positives were 18.0% of alerts for one model (239 alerts, 117 patients) and 38.3% for the other (300
alerts, 105 patients). After remote reprogramming following false alerts, median alerts per day fell
from 0.13 to 0.03 and from 0.15 to 0.01.

In the terms of this module:

- **The burden is in the inbox.** @eq-m38-workload turns these percentages into hours.
- **Premature beats break interval rules.** Irregular intervals are not specific to AF, the same
  failure seen in m37's ectopy test.
- **Fewer alerts is not the whole story.** A study must also report the true events that were not
  sent (@eq-m38-filter), which needs a reference such as continuous recording.

## How experts think

Before trusting an alert rate or a detector's accuracy, ask:

1. **What does the sensor actually time?** A PPG times pulses, not beats (@eq-m38-ibi). Was the
   detector tuned on PPG or on ECG intervals?
2. **What is the unit of the result?** Per window, per notification or per person? @lubitz2022
   reports PPV per detection during patch monitoring; @perez2019 also reports AF in 34% of notified
   participants on a later patch.
3. **What did the rule cost?** Requiring $k$ windows (@eq-m38-runs) lowers false notifications but
   misses short episodes (@eq-m38-detect).
4. **Who reviews, and how long does it take?** Turn rates into hours with @eq-m38-workload.
5. **What did the filter hide?** Ask for the share of true alerts kept, by rhythm type, measured
   against a reference (@eq-m38-filter).
6. **Are the windows independent?** Bursts of noise and runs of premature beats break the
   assumption behind @eq-m38-runs.

One sentence to keep: **an always-on detector is judged by its alerts per day and the events it
misses, not by its accuracy on one window.**

## Cheat sheet

| Quantity | Result |
| --- | --- |
| Heart rate (@eq-m38-hr) | $\mathrm{HR} = 60/\overline{\mathrm{IBI}}$ bpm |
| Pulse intervals (@eq-m38-ibi) | $\mathrm{IBI}_i = RR_i + \Delta_{i+1} - \Delta_i$ |
| Pulse-interval variance (@eq-m38-ibi-var) | $\operatorname{Var}(\mathrm{IBI}) = \operatorname{Var}(RR) + 2\sigma_\Delta^2(1-\rho)$ |
| False notifications (@eq-m38-runs) | $\mathbb E[\text{runs}] = q^k[1 + (n-k)(1-q)]$ |
| Episode caught (@eq-m38-detect) | $1 - a_L$, with $a_m = \sum_{j<k} p^j(1-p)a_{m-j-1}$ |
| Review load (@eq-m38-workload) | $A = N\lambda$, false $N\lambda(1-\mathrm{PPV})$, hours $N\lambda\tau/60$ |
| After a triage filter (@eq-m38-filter) | $\mathrm{PPV}' = \kappa\mathrm{PPV}/[\kappa\mathrm{PPV} + (1-r)(1-\mathrm{PPV})]$; lost $N\lambda\mathrm{PPV}(1-\kappa)$ per day |

**Published numbers used in this module**

| Study | Design | Result |
| --- | --- | --- |
| @perez2019 | 419,297 smartwatch users | 0.52% notified; AF in 34% of notified participants with an analyzable patch |
| @lubitz2022 | 455,699 tracker users; 11 consecutive irregular 5-min windows | Detection PPV 98.2% (95% CI 95.5–99.5%) for concurrent AF |
| @neiman2024 | ILRs in a surveillance program | Historical false alerts about 75%; 18.0% and 38.3% for two newer models |
| @covino2024 | Systematic review, 3,305 ILR patients | False alarms 59.7% of remote transmissions |

**Rules of thumb**

- Multiply per-window rates by windows per day before judging them.
- Each extra window in "k in a row" divides false notifications by about $1/q$.
- Quote a filter's kept-true share next to its removed-false share.

## Interview questions

Try each question before you open its model answer. In a real interview, say which assumptions you
are making.

**Q1. Why are intervals between PPG pulses more variable than RR intervals, even in perfectly regular
rhythm?**

<details class="model-answer">
<summary>Model answer</summary>

Each pulse arrives a delay $\Delta_i$ after its R peak, and that delay varies. Then
$\mathrm{IBI}_i = RR_i + \Delta_{i+1} - \Delta_i$ (@eq-m38-ibi), so even constant RR intervals give
varying pulse intervals. With stationary delays independent of RR,
$\operatorname{Var}(\mathrm{IBI}) = \operatorname{Var}(RR) + 2\sigma_\Delta^2(1 - \rho)$,
which is @eq-m38-ibi-var. Motion artifacts add missed and extra pulses on top.

</details>

**Q2. Derive the expected number of false notifications for a "k windows in a row" rule.**

<details class="model-answer">
<summary>Model answer</summary>

Count runs by where they start. A run of at least $k$ starts at window 1 if windows 1 to $k$ are all
positive: probability $q^k$. It starts at window $i > 1$ if window $i-1$ is negative and windows $i$
to $i+k-1$ are positive: probability $(1-q)q^k$, for $n - k$ values of $i$. Summing gives
$q^k[1 + (n-k)(1-q)]$ (@eq-m38-runs). Each run is counted once, at its start.

</details>

**Q3. With 288 windows a day and $q = 0.05$, roughly how many false notifications a day for $k = 1$
and $k = 3$?**

<details class="model-answer">
<summary>Model answer</summary>

$k = 1$: $0.05[1 + 287 \times 0.95] \approx 13.7$ a day. $k = 3$:
$0.05^3[1 + 285 \times 0.95] \approx 1.25 \times 10^{-4} \times 271.75 \approx 0.034$ a day, about one
a month (@eq-m38-runs). Each extra window divides the rate by roughly 20 here.

</details>

**Q4. What does requiring more windows in a row cost?**

<details class="model-answer">
<summary>Model answer</summary>

Short episodes. An episode of $L$ windows is caught with probability $1 - a_L$ (@eq-m38-detect),
which falls as $k$ rises, sharply once $k$ approaches $L$, and is zero for $L < k$. If short
episodes matter for the purpose of monitoring, a large $k$ hides them. Demo m38-d1 shows both
curves together.

</details>

**Q5. A wearable study reports a positive predictive value of 98%. Another reports AF in 34% of
notified people. Can both be right?**

<details class="model-answer">
<summary>Model answer</summary>

Yes, because they answer different questions. @lubitz2022 reports the PPV of a detection that
occurred while an ECG patch was worn, for AF at the same time. @perez2019 reports how many notified
participants had AF anywhere on a patch applied on average 13 days later; paroxysmal AF may simply
not occur during the patch. Always ask what the numerator and denominator are, and when the
reference was recorded.

</details>

**Q6. A clinic follows 500 ILR patients with 0.1 alerts per patient per day, 25% of them true, 3
minutes each. What is the daily load?**

<details class="model-answer">
<summary>Model answer</summary>

50 alerts a day, 37.5 of them false, and $50 \times 3/60 = 2.5$ hours of review (@eq-m38-workload).
The load depends on the alert rate and review time, not on how many patients are ill.

</details>

**Q7. A triage filter removes 70% of false alerts and keeps 98% of true ones. Starting from a PPV of
25%, what is the new PPV, and what is lost?**

<details class="model-answer">
<summary>Model answer</summary>

$\mathrm{PPV}' = 0.98 \times 0.25 / (0.98 \times 0.25 + 0.3 \times 0.75) = 0.245/0.47 \approx 0.52$,
by @eq-m38-filter. Shown alerts fall to 47% of the original. 2% of true alerts are hidden: in the Q6
clinic, $12.5 \times 0.02 = 0.25$ a day, about 7.5 a month, which no one reviews.

</details>

**Q8. Why do premature beats cause false AF alerts, and what feature could help?**

<details class="model-answer">
<summary>Model answer</summary>

Interval-based detectors see irregular RR intervals, and premature beats produce them; the review
by @covino2024 found premature beats the main cause of false AF alarms. Features that use atrial
activity (P waves on an ECG, or electrogram morphology in devices) can separate them, as can
patterns of intervals: a premature beat is usually followed by a longer interval, while AF intervals
vary without that pattern.

</details>

**Q9. The independence assumption behind @eq-m38-runs fails in practice. In which direction is the
error?**

<details class="model-answer">
<summary>Model answer</summary>

False windows cluster: noise, motion and runs of premature beats last longer than one window. With
positive correlation, runs of $k$ false windows are more likely than $q^k$ suggests, so the formula
underestimates false notifications. Measure the lag-one correlation of window flags on real data,
as lab part E does, before trusting the formula.

</details>

**Q10. How would you evaluate an AI filter for ILR alerts before using it in a clinic?**

<details class="model-answer">
<summary>Model answer</summary>

Run it silently on all alerts, with every alert still reviewed by staff, for long enough to see rare
rhythms. Report $\kappa$ (true alerts kept) and $r$ (false alerts removed) with confidence
intervals, by rhythm type. Count review hours saved (@eq-m38-workload, @eq-m38-filter). Look at every
true alert the filter would have hidden. Decide in advance which losses are acceptable. Module m45
covers silent deployment and monitoring.

</details>

**Q11. A model trained on intracardiac electrograms separates AF from atrial tachycardia well. Why
might that matter for implanted devices?**

<details class="model-answer">
<summary>Model answer</summary>

Devices tend to group AF, flutter and atrial tachycardia as high-rate events, which can delay or
misdirect therapy [@rodrigo2022]. A classifier that separates them could make alerts more specific.
In that study, rule-based classifiers using rate or regularity misclassified about 10–12% of cases.
It would still need testing on device-recorded signals and in prospective use.

</details>

**Q12. Where could an AI agent help a remote-monitoring clinic, and where must it not act?**

<details class="model-answer">
<summary>Model answer</summary>

It could gather each transmission, run validated detectors as tools, pull the patient's history and
pre-fill the review form, so a person decides faster. Numbers must come from the tools, not from the
language model [@feli2025]. It must not dismiss alerts on its own or change device programming;
every action that changes something goes through a person. Module m44 treats this design.

</details>

## Code lab

The lab times pulses against beats, tests the consecutive-window rule, simulates a review inbox and
then tries the rule on real Holter recordings. It runs in about a minute.

| Part | What you do | Data |
| --- | --- | --- |
| A | Build ECG and PPG timing; check @eq-m38-ibi and @eq-m38-ibi-var | synthetic |
| B | A windowed irregularity detector on a day of rhythm: estimate $q$ and $p$ | synthetic |
| C | The k-in-a-row rule: simulate days and episodes; check @eq-m38-runs and @eq-m38-detect | synthetic |
| D | A clinic inbox with a triage model: review hours and hidden true alerts (@eq-m38-workload, @eq-m38-filter) | synthetic |
| E | The same detector on Holter beat annotations; how correlated are false windows? | PhysioNet |
| F | Optional: a small network on RR-interval windows, in PyTorch | synthetic |

- **Python notebook:**
  [labs/python/m38_lab.ipynb]({{< var repo.url >}}/blob/main/labs/python/m38_lab.ipynb).
  Run it from the course repository after `pip install -r requirements.txt`, or
  [open it in Google Colab]({{< var repo.colab >}}/blob/main/labs/python/m38_lab.ipynb).
- **Data for part E:** beat (.qrs) and rhythm (.atr) annotations of five records of the MIT-BIH
  Atrial Fibrillation Database [@afdb; @goldberger2000] (Open Data Commons Attribution v1.0), a few
  hundred kilobytes, downloaded from PhysioNet and checked against its published SHA-256 list.
  Without internet access, part E is skipped.
- **Part F** runs only if PyTorch is installed (`pip install torch`).

Each part ends with **checks**: lines that pass with the code as given. If you change something
and a check fails, that is information, not an error to hide.

## Self-check

Short checks you can do in your head. Open each answer after you have tried it.

**S1. Mean pulse interval 0.75 s. Heart rate?**

<details class="model-answer">
<summary>Answer</summary>

$60/0.75 = 80$ beats per minute (@eq-m38-hr).

</details>

**S2. Pulse delays vary with SD 20 ms and no correlation between beats. By how much does the
variance of pulse intervals exceed that of RR intervals?**

<details class="model-answer">
<summary>Answer</summary>

$2 \times (0.020)^2 = 0.0008\ \mathrm{s}^2$, an extra SD of about 28 ms (@eq-m38-ibi-var).

</details>

**S3. True or false: with $k = 1$, the expected number of notifications is about $nq$.**

<details class="model-answer">
<summary>Answer</summary>

Almost: $q[1 + (n-1)(1-q)]$, slightly less than $nq$, because neighbouring positive windows merge
into one run (@eq-m38-runs).

</details>

**S4. An AF episode lasts 3 windows and the rule needs 4. Chance of catching it?**

<details class="model-answer">
<summary>Answer</summary>

Zero: $a_m = 1$ for $m < k$ (@eq-m38-detect).

</details>

**S5. A filter keeps every true alert and removes no false ones. What happens to PPV?**

<details class="model-answer">
<summary>Answer</summary>

Nothing: with $\kappa = 1$ and $r = 0$, $\mathrm{PPV}' = \mathrm{PPV}$ (@eq-m38-filter).

</details>

**S6. Doubling the number of patients followed, with the same alert rate, does what to review
hours?**

<details class="model-answer">
<summary>Answer</summary>

Doubles them (@eq-m38-workload).

</details>

## Literature figures

These figures are worth looking at alongside this module. We link to them instead of copying them:
some licenses do not allow reuse here, and others we could not confirm. Each entry says what to
look for and where this module explains it.

- **Notification, confirmation and PPV by subgroup.** Lubitz and colleagues, Figure 2 [@lubitz2022;
  [free full text](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC9640290/)]. Three panels: the share of
  participants notified, the share of notified participants with AF or flutter on a later patch,
  and the detection's PPV against a patch worn at the same time. Each panel has a different
  denominator (interview Q5).
- **How long the AF lasted.** Lubitz and colleagues, Figure 3 [@lubitz2022]. AF burden on the patch
  among participants with confirmed arrhythmia, and the duration of the longest episode. Compare with
  what a "k in a row" rule can catch (@eq-m38-detect).
- **Alert transmissions per patient.** Neiman and colleagues, Figure 1 [@neiman2024;
  [free full text](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC10944033/)]. Mean alert transmissions
  per patient, among patients with at least one alert, for the two ILR models. Turn them into
  review hours with @eq-m38-workload.
- **The algorithm behind a smartwatch notification.** Perez and colleagues describe the algorithm
  and how pulse intervals (tachograms) were sampled in their supplementary appendix [@perez2019;
  [free full text](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC8112605/)]. Look for the windowing and
  the confirmation rule, and compare them with @eq-m38-runs.

## Further reading

- **PPG.** @allen2007: a review of photoplethysmography, its signal and its clinical uses.
- **Wearable studies.** @perez2019 and @lubitz2022: two large prospective studies of
  notification algorithms.
- **Implanted monitors.** @covino2024 (false alarms, systematic review), @neiman2024 (AI-based
  detection in practice) and @antoun2025 (AI across implanted devices).
- **Device electrograms.** @rodrigo2022.
- **Data.** @afdb, with @goldberger2000 for PhysioNet.
- **Agents.** @feli2025 and @iwai2025, and module m44.
